title: How Good Is the Fit? Residuals and Correlation

steps.body: Once a line is fitted, every point has a **residual**: its actual value minus what the line predicted. A point above the line has a positive residual; a point below has a negative one. Small residuals, scattered on both sides, mean the line is doing its job.
Refit the hours-vs-score line from before.

predict.prompt: The hours-studied scatter clusters tightly around its fitted line. Will the residuals mostly be small, or mostly be large?

options.label: Small — the points hug the line closely
Large — a tight cluster still leaves big gaps

predict.reveal: Small. A tight cluster around the line means every point's actual value is close to what the line predicted — that closeness IS what a small residual is. A point 0.3 above the fitted line has a small residual even if its nearest neighbour sits far along the line; a point 8 below it would have a large one — the gap that counts runs vertically to the line, not between the points.

widget.prompt: Fit the line again: hours studied (x) versus test score (y).
widget.successFeedback: y = 5x + 60 again. Now look at the gaps: none of the six points sit far from this line — the whole point of fitting well is keeping every one of those gaps small.
widget.slopeFeedback: The tilt is off for this trend.
widget.offsetFeedback: The tilt is right; slide the line toward the middle of the cloud.

explanationVariants: At x = 3, predicted is 5(3)+60 = 75; actual is 74; residual is 74 − 75 = −1.
Residual is always actual minus predicted, in that order.

widget.prompt: At x = 3, the line predicts y = 5(3) + 60 = 75, but the actual score was 74. What is the residual?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 has the right size but the wrong sign — actual (74) is BELOW predicted (75), so the residual is negative.
75 is the predicted value itself, not the gap. Residual = actual − predicted = 74 − 75.

steps.body: Read what a residual's size says.
explanationVariants: A residual near 0 means the line predicted that point almost exactly.
The residual's SIZE (distance from 0) is what measures the miss — sign just says which direction.

widget.prompt: A residual of −1, compared to a residual of −15 on the same scale, tells you the line's prediction was:

options.label: Much closer for the −1 point than the −15 point
options.feedback: Smaller size means a smaller miss. −1 is a near-exact prediction; −15 is a much bigger gap, even though both are negative.

options.label: Equally close, since both are negative
options.feedback: Sign only says WHICH side of the line the point fell on. Size is what measures how far off the prediction was.

options.label: Worse for the −1 point
options.feedback: Backwards — a residual's magnitude is the miss; 1 is a smaller miss than 15.

options.label: Impossible to compare without more information
options.feedback: The two numbers alone are enough: compare their sizes directly.

steps.body: Checking every residual by hand doesn't scale. The **correlation coefficient**, r, compresses that whole pattern into one number from −1 to 1: close to ±1 means the residuals are tiny and the points hug the line; close to 0 means the points are scattered with barely any linear trend at all. The sign matches the slope's direction; the SIZE says how strong the relationship is.
A noisier dataset, same rough upward trend. Fit what you can.

widget.prompt: Fit a line to this noisier upward trend.
widget.successFeedback: A trend is there, but every point sits noticeably farther from the line than in the tidy dataset — bigger residuals throughout. That is exactly the picture of a WEAKER correlation, even with the same general direction.
widget.slopeFeedback: Keep adjusting — some tilt fits this noisier trend better than others, even if no tilt fits perfectly.
widget.offsetFeedback: Slide toward the middle of this messier cloud.

steps.body: Compute r from the summary sums — the formula every calculator runs.
explanationVariants: Build the numerator and the two denominator pieces separately, then divide.

widget.prompt: For 5 points: Σx=15, Σy=25, Σxy=83, Σx²=55, Σy²=135. Compute r using r = [nΣxy−ΣxΣy] / √([nΣx²−(Σx)²][nΣy²−(Σy)²]). (2 decimals)

commonErrors.feedback: 1.6 skips the square root in the denominator — divide by √(50×50), not by 50 alone before rooting.
40 is only the numerator. Finish by dividing by the square-rooted denominator: 40/50.

steps.body: Strength is about size, not sign.
explanationVariants: |−0.95| = 0.95 > 0.8, so the negative correlation is actually the STRONGER relationship.
Compare magnitudes to judge strength; the sign only says which direction.
hints: Strip both correlations down to their absolute values before comparing.
0.95 is bigger than 0.8 — the negative one is stronger, just pointed the other way.

widget.prompt: Dataset A has r = 0.8. Dataset B has r = −0.95. Which has the STRONGER linear relationship?

options.label: Dataset B — 0.95 in magnitude beats 0.8
options.feedback: Strength is about |r|, the DISTANCE from 0 — 0.95 is farther from 0 than 0.8, so B's relationship is stronger, even though it runs in the opposite direction.

options.label: Dataset A — positive is always stronger than negative
options.feedback: Sign says direction, not strength. Compare the sizes: 0.95 beats 0.8, regardless of sign.

options.label: They are equally strong since both are 'high'
options.feedback: 0.8 and 0.95 are not equal — 0.95 is closer to 1, meaning a tighter fit.

options.label: Cannot compare a positive and a negative correlation
options.feedback: Comparing magnitudes works precisely because it strips the sign away first.

steps.body: Grading a fit: one gap at a time, then all at once.
takeaways: A residual is actual minus predicted for ONE point — positive above the line, negative below.
The correlation coefficient r, from −1 to 1, summarizes every residual's pattern into a single strength score.
Strength is |r|, the distance from 0 — sign only tells you the direction of the trend.
steps.teaser: next: what a model's slope and intercept mean depends on the story behind the numbers.

concept.body: Rewind. Residual = actual − predicted. If a point's actual value is 50 and the line predicted 45, the residual is 50 − 45 = 5: positive, because the point sits ABOVE the line.

explanationVariants: Subtract predicted from actual, in that order, keeping the sign.

widget.prompt: A point's actual value is 30; the line predicted 34. What is the residual?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 has the right size but the wrong sign — actual is BELOW predicted here, so the residual is negative.
64 adds them. Residual is actual MINUS predicted: 30 − 34.
